segments.line: Let's look at where you just woke up.
It's a longhouse. One single room, about thirty meters long. The
walls are thick timber. The
roof is a layer of birch bark, with grass and earth on top. Turf. A
living roof, about twenty centimeters thick, keeping the heat in like a wool hat.
Outside, the family has shoveled snow up against the walls. On purpose.
Fresh snow can be more than ninety percent trapped air, and trapped air
is exactly what keeps heat from leaking out. The snow is part of the house.
Down the middle of the floor runs the long hearth. A fire pit as long as a car. It's
the heater, the stove, and the only light all at once. And
the chimney? There isn't one. The smoke drifts up and finds its way out through a hole in the roof.
Your eyes sting. Your
hoodie will smell like this for a week.
Along both walls are wide wooden benches. In the day, you sit on them. At
night, you sleep on them. That's the bedroom. All of it. Everyone. Then
you walk to the far end of the house, and the cow from this morning looks up at you. The
animals live under the same roof. A
resting person gives off about a hundred watts of heat. A
cow gives off several times more.
Two cows at one end of the house, and you've got a heater that also makes milk.
Asa pats the cow and says something to you. You're pretty sure it means:
this is our oven.
